Abstract This study analyzes the interaction between IAS 12 (Deferred Taxes), IAS 16 (Depreciation and Amortization), and IAS 36 (Impairment of Assets), assessing their impact on financial statement presentation and corporate tax planning. A quantitative methodology was employed, using a non-experimental, explanatory-level design based on structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The analysis was conducted on accounting data from 50 companies listed in the Superintendencia del Mercado de Valores (SMV) during the period 2022–2024, selected from asset-intensive industries. The empirical results confirmed that depreciation has a significant effect on asset impairment (β = 0.712, p < 0.001) and deferred taxes (β = 0.208, p < 0.001), while asset impairment exerts an even greater influence on deferred taxes (β = 0.803, p < 0.001). The coefficient of determination (R²) for IAS 12 was 0.926, indicating a high explanatory power of the model, while the R² for IAS 36 was 0.506, reflecting moderate predictive power. Factor analysis, external loadings, and discriminant validity confirmed the robustness and reliability of the model structure. These results demonstrate the existence of a systematic relationship between depreciation and amortization policies, impairment losses, and the generation of deferred tax assets and liabilities. The correct application of IAS 16 ensures that the value of assets is allocated objectively over their useful lives, accurately reflecting their ability to generate economic benefits. IAS 36 requires periodic assessments of recoverable amounts, which allows for the timely recognition of impairment losses and avoids overstatements in the financial statements. IAS 12 regulates the accounting treatment of temporary differences resulting from these practices, directly linking management accounting to future tax obligations. The study provides current empirical evidence on the interaction between these standards in SMEs, demonstrating that their coordinated application increases the transparency, reliability, and usefulness of financial information, while improving processes related to tax planning, financial control, and strategic decision-making in accordance with international standards. Keywords: financial reports, accounting measurement, asset valuation, tax strategy, temporary differences, financial indicators 1. Introduction In the field of financial accounting, the correct application of international accounting standards (IASs) is essential to en sure the transparency and comparability of companies' financial information (Edeigba, 2022; Rathke et al., 2019). However, th e interaction between IAS 12 (Deferred Taxes), IAS 16 (Depreciation) and IAS 36 (Impairment of Assets) represents a challenge in accounting management, given that each of these standards regulates key aspects in the measurement, recognition and presentation of financial assets and liabilities (Chavez et al., 2018; Chitta et al., 2023). In particular, the joint impact of depreciation and impairment on the generation of deferred taxes has been the subject of growing interest, as it affects tax planning and the financial stability of companies (Villafuerte, 2023). Despite the importance of these standards, there are gaps in the literature concerning their combined application, which generates uncertainty in accounting and tax decision making (Huaracha, 2019). The background on the interaction of these standards shows that IAS 16 regulates the depreciation of fixed assets, establishing criteria for their recognition and allocation of costs over their useful life (Calozuma et al., 2023; Gonzabay & Suarez, 2022). On the other hand, IAS 36 requires companies to periodically assess the impairment of their assets, determining whether their recoverable value is lower than their book value. This process leads to the recognition of impairment losses, which in turn affects the accounting and tax basis of the company (Chávez, 2020; Junio et al., 2020). Thus, IAS 12 regulates the recognition of deferred taxes, which arise from temporary differences between the book and tax values of assets and liabilities (Pinza-Sanmartín et al., 2020). Recent research has noted that the combination of these three factors generates distortions in Multidiscip. Sci. J. However, most studies have addressed these rules in isolation without analyzing their interaction in financial and tax management (Alejandra et al., 2022; Castillo et al., 2021; Chávez et al., 2020). From a theoretical perspective, this research is based on the theory of accounting measurement, the theory of accounting based on fair value and the theory of temporary differences in deferred taxes, which allow analysis of the interaction between IAS 12, IAS 16 and IAS 36 in the accounting and tax management of companies (Edeigba, 2022; Patsis et al., 2023). Accounting measurement theory establishes the principles governing the valuation and recognition of assets, which are essential for the application of depreciation and impairment (Karapavlović et al., 2020; Rico et al., 2020). Fair value theory supports the restatement of book values, directly affecting the determination of asset impairment and deferred taxes. The theory of temporary differences explains the relationship between accounting and tax variations in the recognition of deferred taxes. With this approach, the study analyzes how the interaction of these accounting standards influences the financial reporting and tax planning of companies. From this perspective, the present study seeks to provide empirical evidence on how the interaction between IAS 12, IAS 16 and IAS 36 impacts financial reporting and tax planning in companies (Edeigba, 2022; Edeigba et al., 2023). From an academic and practical point of view, the justification for this study lies in the need to fill a scientific gap in the accounting and financial literature (Coda et al., 2023; Nguyen, 2024). Although there are studies on the application of each standard individually, the lack of research on their interrelationship limits the ability of companies to anticipate the effects of depreciation and impairment on their tax burden. Moreover, in an economic environment where tax and accounting regulations are constantly evolving, it is imperative to have an analytical framework to assess the impact of these rules on long-term financial planning (Rathke et al., 2019). This study contributes empirical evidence that will be used by accountants, auditors, regulators and academics to improve the understanding and application of these standards in the business context. The novelty of this study lies in its comprehensive approach, which involves simultaneously analyzing the relationships among depreciation, asset impairment and deferred taxes and applying structural equation (SEM) with accounting-financial data from 50 companies during the years 2022, 2023 and 2024. To date, most research has evaluated these standards independently, without considering their joint impact on the financial and tax stability of companies. This analysis allows us not only to understand the interdependence between these factors but also to provide tools to improve accounting management and strategic decision making in organizations from different sectors (Fuentes & Álvarez, 2017; Sierpińska-Sawicz & Sierpińska, 2021). In this sense, the main objective of the research is to analyze IAS 12, IAS 16 and IAS 36 in relation to deferred taxes, depreciation and impairment of assets in companies during the period 2022--2024. The hypotheses that are posed are as follows: H1: Depreciation (IAS 16) has a significant effect on asset impairment (IAS 36). H2: Depreciation (IAS 16) has a significant effect on deferred taxes (IAS 12). H3: Impairment of assets (IAS 36) has a significant effect on deferred taxes (IAS 12). 2. Theoretical framework The analysis of deferred taxes, depreciation and asset impairment from the perspective of IAS 12, IAS 16 and IAS 36 requires a theoretical basis that explains their impact on accounting and financial management (Chávez et al., 2020; Chávez et al., 2018). For this purpose, three fundamental approaches are used: accounting measurement theory, fair value-based accounting theory and the theory of temporary differences in deferred taxes (Liu et al., 2024; Qiao et al., 2023). These theories provide a solid conceptual framework that allows understanding of the importance of the correct application of accounting standards, their influence on financial decision making and the effects that can result from the valuation and recognition of assets and liabilities in financial statements (García et al., 2023; Novillo-Pino & Torres-Palacios, 2021). 3. Accounting measurement theory Petrovic et al. (2016) establishes the fundamentals for the proper valuation of the financial elements in financial statements, ensuring that they accurately reflect the economic situation of an entity. This theory is based on principles such as objectivity, which requires that financial information be impartial and verifiable; prudence, which advises recognizing expenses and liabilities when they are anticipated but revenues only when they are realized; and uniformity, which implies the consistent application of accounting methods over time to allow comparability (De La A Muñoz et al., 2024; Kalusová & Herrmann et al., 2006) These principles are essential for the correct measurement of assets and liabilities, ensuring that the financial statements provide a true and consistent representation of the entity's financial position (Zastawniak, 2024). The application of different measurement bases, such as historical cost and fair value, is justified within this theory to capture diverse economic realities. Historical cost records assets and liabilities at the original acquisition price, providing stability and consistency in financial information (Babaei, 2024). On the other hand, fair value reflects the amounts for which assets could be exchanged or liabilities settled in current transactions between knowledgeable and willing parties, providing a more current perspective of economic value (Kadri et al., 2021; Susanto & Meiryani, 2019). The choice between these https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Rodriguez-Saavedra et al. (2026) 3 measurement bases depends on factors such as the nature of the asset or liability, the purpose of the financial information and the applicable regulatory requirements (Elkemali, 2024). The theory of accounting measurement also serves as a basis for IAS 12, especially with respect to accounting for deferred taxes. Temporary differences between the book and tax values of assets and liabilities give rise to the recognition of deferred tax assets or liabilities (Chávez et al., 2020). That is, the revaluation of an asset under IAS 16 generates a taxable temporary difference if the book value exceeds the tax base, resulting in a deferred tax liability. Likewise, an impairment loss recognized under IAS 36 gives rise to a deductible temporary difference if the tax base of the asset is not adjusted, leading to the recognition of a deferred tax asset. The correct measurement of these deferred taxes is essential to properly reflect the tax implications in financial statements and to ensure that future tax liabilities are recognized accurately (Bagsic et al., 2025; Samuels & Snow, 2024). The theory of accounting measurement also serves as a basis for IAS 12, especially with respect to accounting for deferred taxes. Temporary differences between the book and tax values of assets and liabilities give rise to the recognition of deferred tax assets or liabilities (Chávez, 2020). That is, the revaluation of an asset under IAS 16 generates a taxable temporary difference if the book value exceeds the tax base, resulting in a deferred tax liability. Likewise, an impairment loss recognized under IAS 36 gives rise to a deductible temporary difference if the tax base of the asset is not adjusted, leading to the recognition of a deferred tax asset. The correct measurement of these deferred taxes is essential to properly reflect the tax implications in financial statements and to ensure that future tax liabilities are recognized accurately. In relation to IAS 16, the theory of accounting measurement is manifested in the option to value these assets via either the cost model or the revaluation model. The cost model involves recording the asset at acquisition cost less accumulated depreciation and any impairment losses (Flagmeier, 2022; Octavia et al., 2021). In contrast, the revaluation model allows the value of the asset to be adjusted to its fair value at the date of revaluation, less accumulated depreciation and subsequent impairment losses. This approach ensures that financial statements reflect values that more closely approximate the current economic reality, providing more relevant information to users (Campa et al., 2023; Mura, 2023). Depreciation, on the other hand, systematically distributes the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life, recognizing the wear and tear or consumption of the asset over time (Percevic & Ercegovic, 2023). IAS 36 also builds on accounting measurement theory by requiring entities to periodically assess whether there is an indication that an asset may have suffered an impairment loss (Hamilton, 2023). If such an indication is identified, it is necessary to estimate the asset's recoverable amount, defined as the higher of its fair value is, the lower the costs to sell and its value in use. When the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount, an impairment loss is recognized by adjusting the value of the asset in the financial statements (Rompotis, 2024). This process ensures that assets are not overstated and that the financial statements reflect values that the entity can reasonably recover (Flagmeier & Müller, 2024). 4. Fair value-based accounting theory On the basis of this theory, Hlaing & Pourjalali (2012) refer that financial statements should reflect the current economic value of assets and liabilities instead of their historical cost. This approach seeks to reduce subjectivity in accounting measurement and improve the relevance of the financial information presented to users. Its application has been consolidated in several international accounting standards, including IAS 12, IAS 16 and IAS 36, where the recognition and measurement of deferred taxes, depreciation and impairment of assets depend on the correct determination of fair value (Patsis et al., 2023). Regarding IAS 12, the recognition of deferred taxes is directly influenced by the measurement of assets and liabilities at fair value (Rathke et al., 2019). When an asset is revalued or when its carrying amount is reduced due to impairment, temporary differences are generated between the carrying amount and the tax value, resulting in the recognition of deferred taxes (Abramov et al., 2008). This means that any variation in the value of assets or liabilities affects a company's future tax burden; thus, the application of fair value theory has direct implications for tax planning and financial statement presentation (Chávez et al., 2020). The measurement of deferred taxes under IAS 12, therefore, must consider the volatility in the valuation of assets and liabilities, since changes in their fair value have a significant effect on the company's financial position and its ability to meet its long-term tax obligations (Lepadatu, 2009). The increasing adoption of fair value in accounting standards has generated debates about its impact on financial stability and the predictability of accounting information. Although its application allows financial statements to more accurately reflect market conditions, it also introduces a degree of uncertainty due to the need to estimate future values (Chávez et al., 2018). The relationship of this theory with IAS 16 is manifested in the way in which companies can opt for the revaluation model for the measurement of their fixed assets. By applying this model, assets are periodically adjusted to their fair value on the basis of market conditions, which allows for a more accurate representation of the company's equity position (Edeigba, 2022). This updating of values implies that the financial statements more accurately reflect the productive capacity and income generation potential of the assets, avoiding accounting distortions that could arise with the valuation at historical cost. However, the use of fair value also entails measurement challenges, as it requires the use of estimates and professional judgments to determine the recoverable amount of assets, which influences the volatility of accounting results (Edeigba et al., 2023). The application of this theory in IAS 36 is evident in the treatment of asset impairment (Diehl, 2009). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Rodriguez-Saavedra et al. (2026) 4 Since the standard requires companies to assess whether the carrying amount of an asset exceeds its recoverable amount, fair value less costs to sell or value in use should be used as the benchmark for measurement (Coda et al., 2023). This approach prevents financial statements from reflecting overstated assets, ensuring that their accounting recognition is aligned with the economic reality of the entity. In addition, asset impairment based on fair value allows financial information to be more useful for decision making, as it more objectively shows the capacity of assets to generate economic benefits in the future (Nguyen, 2024). However, the application of fair value in IAS 36 requires companies to perform impairment tests on a regular and consistent basis, which requires the adoption of appropriate valuation methodologies to reliably estimate the recoverable amount of assets (Jin et al., 2022). 5. Theory of temporary differences in deferred taxes According to Jennergren (2010), the theory of temporary differences in referred taxes focuses on the discrepancies that arise between the book and tax values of assets and liabilities, which generate deferred tax obligations or rights. These temporary differences are classified as taxable and deductible. Taxable temporary differences result in deferred tax liabilities, as they involve amounts that will be taxable in future periods when the carrying amounts of assets or liabilities are recovered or settled. On the other hand, deductible temporary differences give rise to deferred tax assets, allowing tax deductions in subsequent periods (García et al., 2023). IAS 12 addresses the accounting treatment of income taxes, emphasizing the need to recognize deferred tax assets and liabilities for all taxable and deductible temporary differences, with specific exceptions (Novillo-Pino & Torres-Palacios, 2021). In other words, when revaluing an asset under IAS 16, if the book value exceeds the tax base, a taxable temporary difference arises that requires the recognition of a deferred tax liability. This approach ensures that the future tax implications of current transactions are adequately reflected in financial statements, providing a more accurate picture of the entity's future tax obligations (Kulikova et al., 2018). On the basis of IAS 16, temporary differences arise when there is a discrepancy between the carrying amount of an asset and its tax base. In other words, if an entity opts for the revaluation model and increases the carrying amount of an asset, this revaluation is not always immediately reflected in the tax base, creating a taxable temporary difference. This situation generates the need to recognize a deferred tax liability, reflecting the taxes that will be payable when the carrying amount of the asset is recovered (Kalusová & Badura, 2022). This treatment ensures that financial statements consider the future tax consequences arising from asset revaluation decisions (Anggraeni et al., 2020; Mear et al., 2020). IAS 36 also interacts with the theory of temporary differences in deferred taxes. When an impairment loss is recognized, the carrying amount of an asset is reduced, but this decrease may not immediately affect the tax basis of the asset, giving rise to a deductible temporary difference (Novotná & Volek, 2023). This difference results in the recognition of a deferred tax asset, as the entity will be able to deduct the loss for tax purposes in future periods. This treatment ensures that future tax benefits associated with impairment losses are reflected in the current financial statements, aligning the reported tax charge with the economic reality of the entity (Soliman & Ali, 2020). 6. Materials and methods The present research was of an applied type (Prince & Yrrazabal, 2019) and correlational-explanatory level, with a quantitative approach, based on the analysis of accounting-financial data of 50 companies during the years 2022, 2023 and 2024, with the purpose of evaluating the relationships among depreciation (IAS 16), asset impairment (IAS 36) and deferred taxes (IAS 12). A nonexperimental, longitudinal and retrospective design was used since no variables were manipulated and the effects were analyzed over a period of three years, observing the evolution of accounting indicators in companies in regulated sectors (Flagmeier & Müller, 2024). For data collection, the documentary analysis technique was applied, collecting information from audited financial statements, explanatory notes and accounting reports of each company, ensuring the correct application of IAS 12, 16 and 36. The sample was selected under nonprobabilistic convenience sampling, choosing companies that presented complete financial statements and reported information on depreciation, asset impairment and deferred taxes (Bonilla, 2024). Sectors with intensive use of fixed assets, such as manufacturing, construction, mining and energy, were included, considering both companies listed on the Lima Stock Exchange (BVL) and those with accessible data at the Superintendencia del Mercado de Valores (SMV). The data collected were organized in structured data matrices in Excel and SPSS and subsequently analyzed via structural equation (SEM) in SmartPLS. For this purpose, depreciation, asset impairment and deferred taxes were defined as latent variables, each with their respective observable indicators extracted from financial statements (Rompotis, 2024). The relationships between these variables were evaluated via structural models, regression coefficients and statistical significance tests to determine the impact of accounting management on the fiscal planning and financial stability of companies (Rodriguez-Saavedra et al., 2025). To strengthen the validity of the study, a methodological triangulation was used, combining quantitative analysis with SEM, review of accounting standards (IAS 12, 16 and 36) and comparison with previous studies on the application of these standards in different industries. This approach made it possible https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Rodriguez-Saavedra et al. Discussion The interaction between NIC 12, NIC 16, and NIC 36 demonstrates an accounting framework that is critical for effective financial and fiscal governance. The results of the PLS-SEM structural model revealed a high coefficient of determination (R² = 0.926) for IAS 12, indicating that most of the variance in deferred taxes is explained by the independent variables. This finding is consistent with Flagmeier (2022) argument that deferred taxes provide significant informational value when timing differences are properly recognized. Similarly, the study by Campa et al. (2023) supports the conceptual validity of recognizing these taxes as effective tools for strategic tax planning, insofar as they reflect the financial impact of amortization and impairment policies. Regarding IAS 16, empirical evidence highlighted a strong influence on IAS 36 (β = 0.712) and a smaller, but significant, impact on IAS 12 (β = 0.208). These results are consistent with the conclusions of García et al. (2023), who point out that amortization methods directly affect the assessment of asset impairment by influencing residual book values. Similarly, Calozuma et al. (2023) emphasize that the correct application of depreciation improves the quality of financial information and https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Rodriguez-Saavedra et al. (2026) 8 mitigates asset overvaluation. The insignificant burden of the “useful life” indicator (p = 0.435) in this study is consistent with the concerns of Nguyen (2024), who warns that subjective estimates of useful life can compromise objectivity in the measurement of impairment. With regard to IAS 36, the analysis showed a strong relationship with IAS 12 (β = 0.803), suggesting that impairment losses have a direct effect on the recognition of deferred taxes. This finding is consistent with the observations of Novillo-Pino and Torres-Palacios (2021), who analyzed the post-COVID-19 context and highlighted that recoverable value reductions lead to significant adjustments to tax liabilities. This link is supported by Coda et al. (2023), who argue that the high quality of information disclosed under IAS 36 allows for the anticipation of tax contingencies arising from impairment, reinforcing the relevance of impairment testing for accurate tax reporting. Furthermore, reliability analysis (Cronbach's alpha > 0.8) and the convergent validity of the model validate the structural soundness of the constructs of IAS 12 and IAS 36. This supports the conclusions of Edeigba et al. (2023), who highlight the importance of consistent measurement of temporary differences, especially when they are influenced by accounting adjustments to non-current assets. Similarly, Bonilla (2024) emphasizes that greater transparency in the treatment of deferred taxes and impairment improves financial risk management. The empirical results obtained confirm that the statistical model used is appropriate for analyzing the tax consequences of accounting decisions. Finally, the analysis of the f² effects revealed that IAS 36 has a substantial influence on IAS 12 (f² = 4.309), while IAS 16 has a more limited effect (f² = 0.290). This classification of effects underscores that impairment decisions are crucial for estimating deferred tax liabilities, in line with Mura (2023), who points out that impairment adjustments, by altering the carrying amount of assets, have immediate consequences for the tax base. Overall, the results underscore the advantage of examining the interactions between these standards using robust statistical models, which improves the transparency and usefulness of financial statements and contributes to more effective tax supervision. 9. Conclusions This study confirmed the existence of a significant relationship between depreciation, asset impairment, and deferred taxes, establishing their combined impact on the presentation of financial statements and tax obligations. Depreciation of assets directly influences their impairment, requiring companies to conduct periodic reviews to determine recoverable value and avoid overstatements in financial statements. The correct application of IAS 16 is essential to ensure that depreciation objectively reflects the useful life of assets and their ability to generate economic benefits, supporting reliable and transparent accounting practices. In addition, depreciation generates temporary differences that affect deferred taxes, albeit to a lesser extent. This highlights the need to properly manage the reconciliation between the accounting basis and the tax basis, considering the guidelines of IAS 12 to avoid tax contingencies. In this regard, it is necessary to integrate tax criteria into accounting processes, and tax planning should incorporate strategies that optimize the recognition of deferred taxes without distorting financial information. Consistency between accounting and tax treatments contributes to better alignment with international standards and facilitates regulatory compliance. On the other hand, asset impairment showed a significant relationship with deferred taxes, demonstrating that the recognition of impairment losses has a direct effect on the future tax burden. The application of IAS 36 is key in this process, as it ensures that the valuation of assets reflects their actual recoverability, avoiding unnecessary adjustments in taxation. In this context, impairment testing becomes a strategic tool not only for financial reporting but also for anticipating tax effects, especially in scenarios of economic uncertainty or asset impairment. Overall, the findings of this research highlight the importance of integrated application of IAS 12, IAS 16, and IAS 36 to strengthen the consistency, accuracy, and tax relevance of financial reporting. Such integration enables companies to make more informed decisions regarding asset management, improve internal control, and ensure compliance with tax obligations under international financial reporting frameworks. JSON: Name: ias_depr_imp_tax_sem Title: PLS-SEM analysis of the effects of depreciation and asset impairment on deferred taxes in asset-intensive companies Short Hypothesis: More aggressive depreciation policies (higher depreciation expense or revaluation choices under IAS 16) cause increased recognized asset impairment (IAS 36), which in turn cause larger deferred tax balances (IAS 12) in asset-intensive companies. Related Work: Existing empirical work primarily evaluates IAS 12, IAS 16, and IAS 36 in isolation using linear regressions, event studies, case analyses, or descriptive comparisons. Regression-based studies quantify pairwise associations (e.g., depreciation→taxes or impairment→taxes) but often treat measurement error in disclosed indicators as negligible and ignore latent-construct structure. Case studies provide depth on individual accounting choices but lack generalizability. A minority of studies apply structural models, but they typically use small cross-sectional samples, do not test mediation paths explicitly, or omit comprehensive reliability and discriminant-validity assessments. Covariance-based SEM applications are rare and often infeasible with non-normal financial-disclosure indicators; predictive validity checks (PLS predictive tests or out-of-sample prediction) are seldom reported. Across these approaches the common limitations are: lack of joint modeling of interdependent standards, limited longitudinal analysis, inconsistent indicator construction, insufficient validity/reliability reporting, and weak treatment of potential endogeneity and measurement-model choice. Abstract: This research formulates and tests a joint structural model of IAS 16 (depreciation), IAS 36 (impairment) and IAS 12 (deferred taxes) to quantify how depreciation policies propagate through impairment recognition to affect deferred tax balances in asset-intensive firms. We apply partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to a three-year panel of audited financial statements, modeling depreciation, impairment and deferred taxes as latent constructs built from disclosed indicators. The main contribution is an empirically validated mediation model that isolates direct and indirect effects of depreciation policy on deferred taxes and reports construct reliability, discriminant validity, and predictive performance. Expected outcomes are robust estimates of path coefficients, high explanatory power for deferred taxes when impairment is included as a mediator, and evidence that indicator selection and measurement-model choices materially alter effect sizes. The results aim to inform accounting practice and tax planning by clarifying the quantitative linkages among these international standards. Experiments: Dataset: audited financial statements and explanatory notes for N=50 asset-intensive companies (manufacturing, construction, mining, energy) over three years (2022–2024) obtained from the SMV/BVL public filings; panel-level dataset with company-year observations (T=3). Indicators and latent constructs: IAS_16 (depreciation_method [binary: revaluation=1/cost=0], depreciation_expense, residual_value, useful_life), IAS_36 (impairment_loss, impairment_reversal, impairment_test_disclosure), IAS_12 (temporary_differences, deferred_liabilities, tax_credits). Preprocessing: convert nominal policy choices to binaries, winsorize continuous indicators at 1st/99th percentiles, standardize indicators by company size (total assets), impute missing item-level disclosures with indicator-specific mean-imputation flagged by mask. Primary method: reflective PLS-SEM (SmartPLS or R plspm) with bootstrapped significance testing (5,000 bootstrap samples), report path coefficients, t-values, p-values, R2, f2, SRMR. Predictive assessment: PLSpredict with 10-fold cross-validation producing RMSE and MAE per indicator. Baselines: (1) OLS mediation regressions (depreciation→impairment→deferred_taxes) with cluster-robust SEs, (2) covariance-based SEM (lavaan) estimated by ML on same indicators, (3) naive single-equation OLS of depreciation→deferred_taxes. Ablation studies: A1 remove 'useful_life' indicator from IAS_16; A2 alternate IAS_16 measurement from reflective to formative; A3 subgroup analysis: cost-model firms vs revaluation-model firms; A4 panel-aggregation sensitivity: company-level averages vs year-by-year. Evaluation metrics: path coefficients and bootstrap p-values, R2 for endogenous constructs, f2 effect sizes, composite reliability, Cronbach's alpha, AVE, HTMT discriminant validity, SRMR model fit, PLSpredict RMSE/MAE; compare baselines by predictive RMSE and adjusted R2. Statistical tests: pairwise bootstrap difference tests for competing path estimates, Sobel and bootstrap mediation effect estimates with 95% CI. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample size and sampling bias: N=50 firms with T=3 may limit statistical power, external validity, and subgroup inference; nonprobability convenience sampling reduces generalizability. Disclosure heterogeneity: variation in note-level disclosures and inconsistent indicator definitions introduce measurement error and missingness that can bias latent estimates. Construct reliability: some IAS_16 indicators (e.g., useful_life) may have low internal consistency and reduce construct validity. Endogeneity and simultaneity: depreciation choices, impairment recognition, and tax planning may be jointly determined, producing reverse causality not addressable by PLS-SEM alone. Sectoral heterogeneity: industry-specific asset lives and tax treatments limit pooling; subgroup effects may dominate global estimates. Regulatory and tax-rule variability: local tax adjustments or temporary rules can alter temporary-difference mechanics and limit replication across jurisdictions. Model assumptions and identification: reflective vs formative measurement choices materially affect findings; PLS-SEM does not provide the same global goodness-of-fit guarantees as covariance-based SEM. Predictive limits: results may not generalize beyond asset-intensive public firms or different reporting cycles. Computational constraints: bootstrapped PLS with complex formative specifications may require significant compute for stable inference.
